Hatchlings of Emydoidea blandingii emerge from eggs incubated at 30 °C [T = 30 °C] after approximately 55 days [ab = approximately 55 days], a developmental period that falls within the typical range of 45 to 65 days reported for the species under controlled laboratory conditions. At the moment of emergence from the leathery-shelled egg, these neonatal turtles possess a carapace length at birth measuring roughly 3.2 cm [Lb = roughly 3.2 cm], though field surveys have documented a broader range spanning 27 to 39 mm. The wet weight at birth averages 8 grams [Wwb = 8 grams], with individual masses varying between approximately 5.2 and 14 grams depending on clutch origin and maternal condition. This modest body size at hatching reflects the substantial yolk investment required to sustain the hatchling through its initial days of lecithotrophic existence before the onset of exogenous feeding. The relatively small carapace length at birth is typical among emydid turtles and necessitates a prolonged juvenile period during which the growing juvenile must evade predation while building somatic reserves for future maturation.

As juveniles progress toward adulthood, they exhibit a remarkable capacity for sustained growth that ultimately culminates in an impressive ultimate carapace length of 28.7 cm [Li = 28.7 cm] for females. Males, however, attain a considerably smaller adult body size, with an ultimate carapace length for males of 22.3 cm [Li = 22.3 cm], a pronounced sexual dimorphism that is consistent with patterns observed across many emydine turtles. The ultimate wet weight of a fully grown female can reach as much as 5000 grams [Wwi = 5000 grams], representing a more than 600-fold increase over the approximately 8-gram neonatal mass, a trajectory that demands several years of uninterrupted feeding and favorable thermal conditions. In contrast, adult males rarely exceed 2000 grams, their more modest frame reflecting the differing selective pressures operating on each sex. This species thus presents one of the most striking size dimorphisms within the genus Emydoidea, with the asymptotic length of females exceeding that of males by over six centimeters.

Reproductive output in Emydoidea blandingii is highly dependent on the thermal regime experienced by the nesting female during the vitellogenic period. Under conditions where mean environmental temperatures stabilize near 17 °C [T = 17 °C], females produce clutches containing between 12 and 20 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 12 and 20 eggs per clutch], and they typically deposit a single clutch each year [F_R_i = single clutch each year]. This annual reproductive schedule is modest compared to many other freshwater turtles, which often produce multiple clutches within a single active season. The daily reproductive rate implied by these values is very low, a consequence of the extended inter-brood interval and the large individual egg size that characterizes the species. The time since birth at puberty for females is estimated at approximately 2190 days [tp = approximately 2190 days] when individuals are maintained at 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a protracted pre-reproductive period that reflects the substantial energy investment required to build the large body size necessary for successful reproduction. This delayed maturation is typical for a long-lived freshwater turtle with a slow life-history pace.

Male Blanding's turtles follow a distinctly accelerated developmental trajectory relative to females, reaching puberty considerably earlier. At a mean thermal regime of 17 °C [T = 17 °C], the time since birth at puberty for males is only about 1278 days [tp = about 1278 days], which is nearly 900 days earlier than the female pubertal estimate. This sex-specific difference in maturation timing is driven by the smaller ultimate carapace length required of males, which allows them to redirect resources toward gonad maturation at a smaller somatic size. Captive-reared males have been observed producing viable spermatozoa while still substantially below the asymptotic adult carapace length of approximately 22.3 cm, suggesting that sexual maturation is triggered more by age than by the attainment of a critical size threshold. This pattern is consistent with the hypothesis that males benefit from early reproductive activation in a mating system where larger body size confers only limited competitive advantages. The divergence in pubertal timing between sexes is among the most pronounced documented for any emydid turtle.

Longevity records for Emydoidea blandingii indicate an exceptional maximum lifespan of approximately 44 years [am = approximately 44 years] for individuals living under typical environmental conditions near 17 °C [T = 17 °C], a figure that places this species among the longer-lived members of the family Emydidae. This remarkable lifespan, combined with the delayed female sexual maturity of roughly 6 years, produces a reproductive window spanning multiple decades during which a single female can contribute substantially to population recruitment. The species' iteroparous life-history strategy, characterized by modest annual clutch sizes of 12 to 20 eggs and low annual fecundity, is balanced by very high adult survival rates and the capacity for repeated breeding attempts across many seasons. Field studies using mark-recapture techniques have documented individuals exceeding four decades in age, with some senescent animals exhibiting reduced clutch viability in their final years. The physiological mechanisms underpinning this extended lifespan remain poorly understood, though slow somatic growth rates and low metabolic demands are likely contributing factors.
